title: The Hierophant Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Hierophant upright: tradition, learning; reversed: outgrown rules. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Ask your question.
image_alt: The Hierophant, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a figure in a gold triple crown and red robe sits between two grey pillars, right hand raised, crossed gold keys at his feet and two kneeling figures before him.
capsule: The Hierophant, card V of the Major Arcana, stands for tradition, learning, spiritual guidance and shared institutions. Reversed, it means rebellion against rules that no longer fit, or a wish to find your own way. It is a supportive card, though its shadow is conformity. Backed by a tried path and good counsel, its upright answer is yes.

blocks.heading: What is on The Hierophant card?
paragraphs: A robed figure in a tall gold crown sits high between two grey stone pillars, which with him fill most of the card. He wears, as Waite writes, "the triple crown" and is seated "between two pillars, but they are not those of the Temple which is guarded by the High Priestess" (p. 88).

In his left hand is "a sceptre terminating in the triple cross"; with the right he makes what Waite calls "the well-known ecclesiastical sign", one "distinguishing between the manifest and concealed part of doctrine" (p. 88). Then: "At his feet are the crossed keys, and two priestly ministers in albs kneel before him" (p. 88).

On the 1909 card V is printed at the top, the robe is red with a long white band marked with small crosses, and the keys are gold, lying on a red cloth. The two kneeling figures have the crowns of their heads bare and yellow bands crossing their backs; the robe of the one on the left is patterned with red roses.
Waite calls him "the order and the head of the recognized hierarchy" and "the channel of grace belonging to the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature" (p. 91).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Hierophant?
paragraphs: The upright list is about ties between people: some chosen, like marriage and alliance, some that bind against one's will, with mercy and goodness from another account. The reversed words mostly describe getting along, society, concord and good understanding, with over-kindness and weakness as the price.

Waite himself is cooler than the list. He writes that the Hierophant "is not inspiration" (p. 91), although the word appears among the meanings, and he warns that the pontiff may forget "the significance of this his symbolic state" (p. 91).

blocks.heading: What does The Hierophant mean upright?
paragraphs: Tradition and learning are The Hierophant's ground upright: a teacher, a mentor, a school of thought, a community whose values match yours. It often comes up when you do not need to invent a method from scratch, because a tried path already holds much of what you are looking for.

The card favors guidance and shared values. Asking someone experienced, following a proven sequence, joining a group, keeping a ritual that steadies you: all of these belong to it. Its modern meaning also covers religious or spiritual beliefs, formal education and established institutions, from a church to a university or a profession. Waite accepts an earlier description of the card as "the outer side of the life which leads to the doctrine" (p. 91), the visible, shared side of belief.

Its harder side is plain conformity: keeping rules only because everyone does and leaving your own questions unasked. Should either side describe your moment, ask yourself: whose knowledge could spare you a few wrong turns, and which customs would you still choose on your own?

blocks.heading: What does The Hierophant mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The Hierophant can point to rules that no longer fit: customs kept out of habit rather than belief, or the sense of living inside expectations you never agreed to. Most often it means rebellion and freedom, from quiet rebellion, a private wish to find your own way, to openly challenging the status quo and choosing an unconventional path.

Waite's reversed list does not describe rebellion. Its words, society, concord, over-kindness, weakness, sit closer to going along with others too easily, one face of conformity. The rebellious side is a modern reading, not Waite's.
Neither direction is wrong in itself. Ask which beliefs you would still choose today, and keep those on purpose.

blocks.heading: What does The Hierophant mean in love?
paragraphs: Commitment and shared values come to the front when The Hierophant appears in a love reading. It is one of the cards most linked to marriage and to a traditional, committed relationship: promises made seriously and in the open, often with family and community involved. For someone unattached, it may suggest meeting people through a community, a class or a tradition you care about, or working out what kind of commitment you actually want.

Inside a couple, the question is what you are building on together: customs, promises, a way of doing things. Notice whether the familiar shape of a relationship suits you, or whether you would rather design your own.

Reversed, the card can show a pull between what is expected of a relationship and what feels true to you: pressure from family or tradition, different values about commitment, or a wish for a less conventional kind of bond. Which of those expectations are really yours?

blocks.heading: What does The Hierophant mean for work and money?
paragraphs: Career questions with The Hierophant turn toward learning from people who know the field: a mentor, formal training, an established method, the standards of a profession. It can also point to working inside an institution and finding your place in it.

In money terms the card means a conservative, steady approach: tested habits, a budget with clear rules, security built slowly instead of through shortcuts. Reversed, it stands for breaking with how money was always handled, which can bring welcome freedom or careless risk.

blocks.heading: What is The Hierophant's advice?
paragraphs: Ask someone you respect how they would approach the question you are holding, then make the decision yourself. Borrow experience without borrowing a whole life: take the part of a tradition that helps you and leave what does not fit.

blocks.heading: Is The Hierophant a yes or no card?
The Hierophant as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: Read as a figure, The Hierophant is the teacher, the mentor or the keeper of a tradition, someone others come to for counsel; drawn for you, he marks the side of you that teaches or is ready to learn. On a question about someone's feelings, the card traditionally means respect, loyalty and serious intentions: a wish for a committed, conventional bond, often guided more by duty and shared values than by passion. Reversed, it describes feelings held back by expectations: doubts about commitment, a sense of being hemmed in, or a wish for a relationship that does not follow the usual rules.

pairs.text: A personal choice inside shared values. Ask which promise you are ready to keep.
Learning through shared work. Find the person whose craft you want to study up close.
Belonging and celebration. Your community can be a place to learn as well as to rest.
Personal rules meet shared customs. Check which of them you actually agree with.

blocks.heading: The Hierophant or The High Priestess?
paragraphs: The High Priestess also sits between two pillars, and Waite sets the two cards side by side. The Hierophant is "the ruling power of external religion", the High Priestess "the prevailing genius of the esoteric, withdrawn power"; and she "makes no sign" (p. 88), while he raises his hand. Today she is read as intuition and inner knowing, he as tradition and guidance from outside. Looking inward is her territory; looking for a teacher is his.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Hierophant
paragraphs: Who could I learn from on the question I am facing?
Which of my rules did I choose, and which did I simply inherit?
Where do I belong, and what do I bring to that group?

faq.q: Is The Hierophant a good or bad card?
faq.a: Mostly good. The trap it can hide is going along by default, keeping a custom only because everyone does; outside that trap, it stands behind study, steady counsel and the comfort of belonging somewhere.

faq.q: Is The Hierophant the same card as the Pope?
faq.a: Yes. Waite says the card is called "Spiritual Father, and more commonly and obviously the Pope" (p. 14), and that it "seems even to have been named the Abbot" (p. 14). He kept the wider name because the Pope is only "a particular application of the more general office that he symbolizes" (p. 88).

As a meaning, yes; as a prediction, no. Marriage heads Waite's list for this card (p. 284), next to alliance and bonds of duty, and modern readings keep the link to formal, public commitment. The card describes that kind of bond without saying anything certain about a wedding in your own life.

It can be, but it rarely has to be. Waite calls him "not religion, although he is a mode of its expression" (p. 91). In a reading the card usually points to any established system: a school, a profession, a family custom, the beliefs you grew up with.

waite.quote: Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude; by another account, mercy and goodness; inspiration … Reversed: Society, good understanding, concord, over-kindness, weakness.
